15 July 2026

Dear Editors of *Ecology Letters*,

We attach a 300 word proposal for a **Methods** article entitled "A flexible modelling framework for estimating thermal tolerance and sensitivity," for your consideration. 

We develop a new method for deriving thermal tolerance ($CT_{max}$) and sensitivity estimates (i.e., sensitivity slopes, $z$) from dose-response models. We show how this method allows ecologists to model variation directly in these widely used quantities, improving inference and enabling tests of hypotheses that current methods cannot address.  We believe our proposed paper will be of significant interest to the readers of *Ecology Letters*, given the recent high-impact work being published in the journal on the effects of extreme heat [@orsted_suzukii_2024; @orsted2026; @verberk2026]. 

We expect our proposed approach will open up new and more rigorous ways for quantifying and statistically comparing species vulnerability to extreme heat and other dose-dependent anthropogenic stressors. While we have focused on extreme heat, our work also applies to other anthropogenic stressors, such as pesticides, herbicides and other environmental toxins. As such, our contribution will be generally applicable to other fields of research making it highly relevant for the general readership of *Ecology Letters*.  

Thank you for your consideration of our proposal,

Daniel W.A. Noble, Pieter A. Arnold, Shinichi Nakagawa and Patrice Pottier 

-------

Extreme heat is one of the clearest ecological consequences of climate change, but a central bottleneck remains: identifying vulnerable species, populations and processes and predicting extreme-heat impacts in nature [@snook_fertility_2026; @arnold_thermal_2025]. Thermal death time (TDT) and thermal load sensitivity (TLS) models were designed for this task, linking heat intensity, exposure duration and biological failure [@rezende_landscapes_2014; @orsted_finding_2022; @jorgensen_unifying_2021]. Yet, analyses using these models often discard uncertainty, violate model assumptions, handle overdispersion and hierarchy poorly, and make statistically robust group comparisons difficult ([@fig-proposal-framework]A). 

We propose a **Methods** article that provides a direct, flexible replacement while preserving the biological quantities ecologists already use. We develop a new method for deriving thermal tolerance ($CT_{max}$) and sensitivity slopes ($z$) from dose-response models. We show how this method allows ecologists to model variation directly in these widely used quantities, improving inference and enabling tests of hypotheses that current methods cannot address ([@fig-proposal-framework]B). It also enables direct estimates of heat injury and survival in nature, with uncertainty flowing naturally into comparisons and predictions under fluctuating thermal regimes.

Our contribution makes important ecological and statistical advances. Our simulations show that our new modelling approach matches classical estimates when their assumptions hold and is far more reliable when they fail. It also performs much better across common experimental designs in the field. Using empirical case studies in cereal aphids, snow gum, zebrafish and vinegar flies, we show how the framework allows richer questions to be asked that have so far remained elusive.

We make the framework accessible through two documented R packages with tutorials. Importantly, our new method can be generally applied to lethal and sublethal endpoints, count and continuous-proportion data, treatment comparisons and hierarchical designs, making it highly flexible. Building on recent *Ecology Letters* work [@orsted_suzukii_2024; @orsted2026; @verberk2026], it offers a general, uncertainty-aware standard for forecasting biological vulnerability to extreme heat and other dose-response stressors.

![Conceptual comparison of the classical two-stage TDT/TLS workflow and the joint four-parameter log-logistic (4PL) model. (a) In the two-stage workflow, separate dose-response curves are fit at each assay temperature and the resulting $t_{50}$ estimates are regressed against temperature. This workflow can fail when assays do not bracket $t_{50}$, treats first-stage estimates as fixed and independent, and does not naturally propagate uncertainty or account for covariates / hierarchical structure into $z$ and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$. (b) The joint 4PL model estimates the full survival surface in one model. Coloured curves show posterior median survival probabilities at assay temperatures, with shaded pointwise 95% credible intervals. Filled circles mark the model midpoint, `mid(T)`, defining relative $\log_{10}t_{50}$; open triangles mark the absolute 50% survival crossing. A *relative* threshold is each curve's own midpoint (halfway between its lower and upper asymptotes), whereas an *absolute* threshold is a fixed survival probability (here 50%); the two coincide only when the asymptotes are 0 and 1 (see Methods). The black and steelblue trajectories give the relative and absolute $t_{50}$ relationships used to derive $z_\text{rel}$, $z_\text{abs}$, and $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ at the 60-min reference. Dashed curves show the fitted dose response at the corresponding relative and absolute $CT_{max_{1hr}}$ values. Inset: the 4PL parameters `low`, `up`, `mid`, and `k`.
